flows.title: Image to image
flows.summary: Re-render an existing image and control how far it may drift with one slider.
flows.notes: The only difference from a text-to-image request is the source image and the denoising strength that says how far the render may travel from it. The world 1 courier's descriptor block is unchanged between the two renders, so what moves is the weather and nothing else. Denoise sits at 0.70: high enough that the change of weather and light is unmistakable at a glance, and low enough that the subject and the composition survive, which is the balance the lesson is about.

flows.title: Inpainting
flows.summary: Repaint only the masked region of an image, leaving the rest untouched: here, an airship pushed into the sky.
flows.source_note: txt2img/result.webp, downscaled to 512x512; the mask is a rectangle from 0,0 to 285,200 in that frame, the whole sky left of the figure
flows.notes: source_processing must be "inpainting", the model must be an inpainting model, and the mask must match the source dimensions. White is the region that gets repainted. The mask is sent as the lossless PNG beside the result so its binary edge is not softened in transit. Denoise is 1.0 because the studio's inpainting mode has no strength control and submits 1.0: the masked region is replaced outright, so the example must be made of the same request. An inpainting model fills a hole with what its surroundings suggest, so a masked sky comes back as sky unless the prompt is pushed: the subject is written as (a phrase:1.4), which is what makes the airship appear at the same guidance every other example uses. Every inpainting checkpoint the horde serves is SD1.5, so all three worlds render at 512 on an inpainting model: the photoreal and robot worlds on Deliberate Inpainting, the anime world on Anything Diffusion Inpainting.

flows.title: Scannable QR code
flows.summary: Hide a scannable QR code inside a piece of artwork.
flows.notes: The QR payload travels in params.extra_texts with reference "qr_code"; params.workflow selects the QR ControlNet workflow. The prompt asks for weather and nothing geometric on purpose: the ControlNet already carries the code, so a prompt that describes blocks and hard shadows competes with it and what comes out is a barcode with a sky behind it rather than a picture with a code inside it. What the prompt has to supply instead is tone: a torn storm front is light against dark in the same places the code needs to be, which is why this scene scans where a flat haze does not. control_strength is the dial between picture and code, but the public API's payload carries no field for it, so a request through the horde renders at the workflow's own baseline whatever it asks for; that is the 1.0 stated here, and the sweep library's control-strength strip is the same lesson rendered locally, where the dial does move. The published image was decoded with zbar before it shipped: a code that does not scan is not a worked example of anything.

flows.title: Face fixing with GFPGAN
flows.summary: The same seed with and without the GFPGAN post-processor, side by side.
flows.notes: The two requests are identical apart from params.post_processing and params.facefixer_strength, so the pair isolates what the face fixer does. Face fixing is a post-processor, not a sampler setting: it runs on the finished image, so the composition is unchanged and only facial detail is redrawn. World 1 on the photoreal SD1.5 model, where GFPGAN, trained on photographic faces, has the most to give. World 2 shows the same pair on the anime model, where the correction is gentler and the reader can see that it is. World 3 has no variant: the robot has no face to fix, so the first world's pair stands in.

flows.needs_attention: The published pair does not isolate the face fixer and should not be trusted as evidence until it is re-rendered locally. Through the horde runner the before and the after are two independent jobs that land on different workers, so the base renders are not the same image: differencing the published pair puts the change across the whole frame (planks, railing, sky) at roughly the same magnitude as the face, and at 8 steps the coat drape and lighting diverge outright. Only the local runner, which renders both back to back on one GPU, can publish a pair whose sole difference is the post-processor. Also unresolved: ICBINP draws a small face competently, so GFPGAN has little to repair at any framing. Tried through the horde runner, all at seed 1234567890: the published full-body recipe at 30 steps; the same at 12 steps with the close-up/portrait negatives dropped; a three-quarter framing at 30 and at 8 steps; a distant-figure framing at 30 steps with facefixer_strength raised to 1.0; and a 768x512 landscape frame. Every one of them repaired invisibly. To vary next: render locally so the comparison is controlled, then reach for a plainer SD1.5 checkpoint than this face-tuned merge, or a framing that leaves the face genuinely broken. Worlds 2 and 3 have no variant: the anime face is left as it was by GFPGAN (see facefix--w2), and the robot has no face. The first world's pair stands in for both.
